title: Long Division Frame
context: Grade 4, and the method the rest of the chapter is built on. An adult sees a familiar written layout. What is actually at stake is one test, the test for a zero in the quotient. The summary box that follows the worked examples says a zero appears when a digit is not divisible by the divisor. That is the wrong test: the worked examples themselves divide thirty-five and fifty-six by six, neither divisible, and write five and nine. The test the first example states is that the number being divided is smaller than the divisor. A child who follows the box writes a zero at every step that leaves a remainder.

writeup.why: Divide a number place by place from the biggest place down, and find out exactly when a zero belongs in the answer.
writeup.look: A long division frame under place headings, a working window above it naming the place, a multiple strip beside it and a check bar underneath.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Long Division Frame' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the steps finished against the steps this division needs, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each quotient digit settles, zero included, and the second fixed at the number of places being worked. On the last phase it carries the check instead, the rebuilt number against the dividend. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The working window runs across the top of the working area, 640 by 70 at 300,210, holding the number being divided at this step with its place name written after it, fifteen tens and never a bare fifteen. The multiple strip stands at the right, 200 by 510 at 950,210, nine rungs reading the divisor times one to times nine in rose; the largest that fits is dragged to the frame, and a rung bigger than the working number is drawn but will not lift. The frame fills the middle, 640 by 360 at 300,290: place headings from thousands to ones across its top in columns 110 wide, the quotient row directly under the headings, then the bracket with the divisor in amber at its left and the dividend in deep blue under it. Each quotient digit settles above its own place in green; the multiple is written in rose under the working number and taken away, and what is left drops into the left slot, 220 by 64 at 64,300, in vermilion. The bring down arrow beside the next digit stays unlit until the left slot holds a number, and then brings that digit down beside what is left, so the next working number is seen being made. The zero gate is a hinged cover over the quotient cell of the step in hand. It takes a zero only when the working number is smaller than the divisor and writes it in grey at full size; a zero offered at a step that is not smaller is handed back with the rungs of the strip that fit lit, at least the first of them, and the child's offer is written beside the cell. The check bar runs under the frame, 640 by 60 at 300,664, multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder and slides the result under the dividend so the two can be matched digit for digit. The blocks bay stands at the lower left, 220 by 340 at 64,384, three small cards for one block's divisions with a total line under them, its label saying that the block's total is the sum of the three quotients. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient digit, a leftover or a check is asked for. The zero key writes a zero into the cell in hand and nowhere else, and it is the key the gate reads. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A quotient digit never stands anywhere but above its own place, and the place headings never scroll or shrink. A zero the gate has taken is exactly the size of every other digit in the row, because it is holding a place, and a thinner zero is the one that gets left out.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last division the child worked, every quotient digit above its place and every leftover still written, with the check bar matched under the dividend.

phases.win: the first quotient digit lands above its place and what is left is carried to the next place
phases.does: divides the digit in the biggest place, writes the quotient digit above it and says what is left
phases.goal: long division starts with the digit in the biggest place, and what is left is carried on
phases.says: Which place is the biggest? Share that one first.
phases.check: Away from the screen: share nine hundreds, three tens and six ones among four envelopes. Say which notes you shared first and what you changed.
phases.feels: the biggest things go round first, and whatever is left is changed down into the next place rather than thrown away
phases.hands: Hand a group eight hundred-rupee notes, four tens and six ones in play money, and three envelopes. Ask them to share the hundreds first. When two hundreds will not go round, change them for twenty tens and carry on with the tens, then the ones. Then ask what would have happened if they had shared the ones first.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which place is the biggest? Second rung, the phase's: how many of that place does each share get? Third rung: the frame is cut to a two-digit dividend, and the child shares the tens before the ones. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: every written sum this year has started at the ones column, so the right hand end is where the pencil goes first.
wrong.move: starts with the ones, as in adding and taking away, and builds the quotient from the right.
wrong.screen: the working window is set on the ones as the child chose: six ones shared by three gives two, and four tens shared by three gives one ten with one ten left, and that ten has nowhere to go because the ones are already done. The frame then replays the division from the hundreds beside it, the two hundreds left over lit as they are changed into twenty tens and carried on, and both runs stay standing.

wrong.why: the zero feels like the end of the thousands, and nothing written down says the two thousands are still there.
wrong.move: writes a zero for the two thousands of two thousand seven hundred and thirty-six, then divides the seven hundreds on their own as if the two thousands had gone.
wrong.screen: the working window holds the two thousands with their place name and then does not move on alone: the two thousands are changed into twenty hundreds and slide right to join the seven, and the window reads twenty-seven hundreds. The child's seven hundreds stays written above it, and the check bar later rebuilds the child's answer as seven hundred and thirty-six, two thousand short of the dividend.

phases.screen: a frame with the dividend under its place headings and the working window on the biggest place
phases.soWhat: Long division starts with the digit in the biggest place, and what is left is carried on.

phases.win: the working window shows the new number with its place name and the next quotient digit settles
phases.does: fills the left slot, brings the next digit down, and divides the new number in the working window
phases.goal: each step brings down the next digit and divides everything that has built up
phases.says: Say what is left first. Now bring the next digit down. How many is that?
phases.check: Divide seven hundred and twenty-nine by three. Say what is left after each step, before you bring a digit down.
phases.feels: what is left is not finished with, it is the front half of the next number
phases.hands: Work nine hundred and fifty-three divided by four on the board, but stop after every step and ask the class to say what is left before anyone brings a digit down. Write each leftover in coloured chalk beside the next digit. Then rub one leftover out and ask where the next number came from.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is in the left slot? Second rung, the phase's: which digit comes down next, and what does it join? Third rung: the frame is cut to a two-digit dividend with one leftover, and the child fills the slot and brings down once. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the digit brought down is the one the eye is on, and the leftover is written further up the frame, away from it.
wrong.move: divides the five tens on their own and forgets the hundred that was left.
wrong.screen: the child's step is run in the working window as five tens shared by four, one ten each, while the hundred left from the first step stays lit in the left slot, still waiting. The window is then rebuilt with that hundred changed into ten tens and slid beside the five, and it reads fifteen tens; both working numbers stay written, one above the other.

wrong.why: a multiple that fits feels like the right one, and the strip was not climbed to the next rung to see.
wrong.move: takes two fours out of fifteen tens and carries seven tens on, when a third four still fits.
wrong.screen: the seven is written in the left slot as the child gave it and lit against the four at the bracket, seven beside four. The multiple strip lights the rung for three fours, twelve, which still fits under fifteen, and the rung for four fours, sixteen, which does not. The child's two stays beside the quotient cell and the step is offered again, nothing marked.

phases.screen: what is left after the first step, with the next digit waiting and the bring down arrow unlit
phases.soWhat: Each step brings down the next digit and divides everything that has built up.

phases.win: the zero lands above its place and the working number joins the next digit whole
phases.does: compares the working number with the divisor, writes the zero, and carries the whole number on
phases.goal: a zero goes in the quotient only when the number being divided is smaller than the divisor
phases.says: Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then how many fit?
phases.check: In eight hundred and seventeen divided by four, which step gets a zero? The last step leaves one over. Why does it get no zero?
phases.feels: a step with something left over can still fit the divisor several times, and only a number smaller than the divisor fits it none
phases.hands: Share seven hundreds, two tens and five ones among seven envelopes in play money. When only two tens are left to share among seven, ask what each envelope gets in tens, and write the zero. Then share the twenty-five ones. They leave four over, so ask whether that step gets a zero too, and why it does not.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the working number at this step, with its place name? Second rung, the phase's: is it smaller than the divisor? Third rung: the strip is laid against the working number rung by rung from times one, and the child says whether even the first rung fits. The zero key stays open, and the gate still reads it.

wrong.why: the summary box after the worked examples says a zero appears when a digit is not divisible by the divisor, and a step with something left over is exactly what that looks like. The test the first worked example states, smaller than the divisor, never comes into it.
wrong.move: writes a zero in the quotient at every step that leaves a remainder, because that step does not divide exactly.
wrong.screen: the gate hands back the zero offered for nine thousands and the one offered for thirty-six ones, and at each the strip lights the rungs that fit: one seven under nine, five sevens under thirty-six. Only at three tens does the whole strip stay dark, because three is smaller than seven, and there the gate opens and takes the grey zero. The child's zeros stay written beside the cells they were offered for, and the check bar rebuilds the four hundred they would make as two thousand eight hundred, beside the nine thousand eight hundred and thirty-six.

wrong.why: three tens gave nothing to write, and a step that gives nothing feels like a step with nothing to record.
wrong.move: leaves out a zero that belongs, writing one hundred and forty-five remainder one for nine thousand eight hundred and thirty-six divided by seven.
wrong.screen: the check bar multiplies seven by the child's one hundred and forty-five, adds the remainder, and the one thousand and sixteen it rebuilds slides under the dividend a whole place short. The frame is replayed with the gate over the tens cell, the strip stays dark against three tens because three is smaller than seven, the grey zero is taken, and the answer reads one thousand four hundred and five with every place filled.

phases.screen: a step whose working number is smaller than the divisor, with an earlier step that left a remainder still lit
phases.soWhat: A zero goes in the quotient only when the number being divided is smaller than the divisor. Whether the step divides exactly is not the test.
phases.concept: Smaller than the divisor means a zero

phases.win: the rebuilt number slides under the dividend and the two match digit for digit
phases.does: multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder, and lays the result beside the dividend
phases.goal: divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend
phases.says: Multiply the divisor by your answer. Add what was left. Is it the number you started with?
phases.check: Someone says four thousand and nine divided by four is one thousand and two, remainder one. Check it by multiplying back.
phases.feels: the division is undone, and the dividend comes back only when the leftover is put back too
phases.hands: Give each pair a finished division on a card, some right and some with one step wrong. Each pair multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder, and writes the result under the dividend. Ask which cards matched, and on the ones that did not, which step to look at first.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the divisor times the quotient? Second rung, the phase's: what was left at the end, and has it been added? Third rung: the check is cut to twenty-nine divided by four, and the child rebuilds twenty-nine from the answer. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the check is taught as the multiplication undoing the division, and the remainder is not part of any multiplication.
wrong.move: multiplies the divisor by the quotient and forgets to add the remainder.
wrong.screen: the check bar builds eight times six hundred and forty-seven, five thousand one hundred and seventy-six, and slides it under the dividend, where the ones do not match. The remainder is then lifted out of its slot and added on, the rebuilt number becomes five thousand one hundred and seventy-eight, and it matches digit for digit. Both rebuilt numbers stay drawn.

wrong.why: each subtraction in the working checks out on its own, and a step that was never written leaves no mark to look at.
wrong.move: accepts eighty-four remainder two for seven thousand five hundred and sixty-two divided by nine, because every step shown was right.
wrong.screen: the check bar builds nine times eighty-four, adds two, and the seven hundred and fifty-eight it makes slides under the dividend a whole place short. The frame is replayed step by step, and at the ones the two left is smaller than nine, so the gate takes the grey zero in the ones place. The check runs again on eight hundred and forty remainder two and matches digit for digit.

phases.screen: a finished division with the check bar empty under it
phases.soWhat: Divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the working number is smaller than the divisor. The gate lifts, the whole strip of multiples lights and then goes dark rung by rung from the top down, because not even the first rung fits, and the grey zero drops into the quotient cell at full size. Then the working number does not fall away: it slides right, whole, and the next digit comes down beside it, so three tens and six ones become thirty-six ones in front of the child. It can be replayed as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the frame holds the dividend under its place headings with the divisor behind the bracket, the quotient row empty, and the working window above the frame lit on the biggest place with its place name. On the second the first quotient digit already stands above its place and its multiple has been taken away, the left slot is empty, and the bring down arrow is drawn unlit beside the next digit. On the third the division has reached a step whose working number is smaller than the divisor, the gate is closed over that quotient cell, and an earlier step that left something over is still lit. On the fourth a finished division stands whole with the check bar empty under it. The running count at the top left holds the steps finished against the steps the division needs, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the biggest place heading, or the empty left slot, or the gate, or the empty check bar, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which place goes first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any dividend up to four digits and any divisor from two to nine, with the working window, the zero gate, the check bar and the blocks bay open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on starting with the biggest place, bringing down and dividing again, writing a zero only when the number is smaller than the divisor, and checking by multiplying back.
voiceLines: A number under its place headings, and a divisor at the door. Which place goes first?
Which place is the biggest? Share that one first.
Say what is left first. Now bring the next digit down. How many is that?
Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then how many fit?
Multiply the divisor by your answer. Add what was left. Is it the number you started with?
A new division. Name the biggest place before anything is shared.
Free play. Any dividend, any divisor from two to nine, with the gate and the check bar open.
Read the working window with its place name, then lay the multiples beside it.
Every step said, every zero where the number was smaller, and every check matched.

observations.why: Sharing the biggest things first leaves the smaller places free to take whatever is changed down into them.
observations.soWhat: Long division starts with the digit in the biggest place and carries what is left into the next place.
observations.observe: The first quotient digit landed above the biggest place, and what was left went on to the next place rather than away.

observations.why: What is left joins the next digit, so the next number to divide cannot be made without it.
observations.soWhat: Say what is left at every step, because it is the front half of the next number.
observations.observe: The bring down arrow would not light until the left slot held a number.

observations.why: A zero means no divisor fits at all, which happens only when the number is smaller than the divisor, and a step with something left over can still fit it several times.
observations.soWhat: The test for a zero is smaller than the divisor. A step that is not divisible but not smaller still gets a digit of one or more.
observations.observe: The gate took a zero at one step and handed it back at another step that left something over.

observations.why: Divisor times quotient counts every share handed out, and the remainder adds back what was never handed out.
observations.soWhat: Multiplying back and adding the remainder checks a division, and leaving the remainder off makes a right answer look wrong.
observations.observe: The rebuilt number slid under the dividend and matched it digit for digit.

description: Divide place by place from the biggest place down, say what is left at each step, and write a zero only when the number is smaller than the divisor.

source_tool.description: A long division frame fills the stage, the dividend written under place headings from thousands to ones and the divisor standing at its left behind the bracket. A working window above the frame shows the number being divided at each step together with its place name, so fifteen tens is shown as fifteen tens and not as a bare fifteen. A multiple strip beside the window lists the divisor times one up to times nine, and the child picks the largest that fits. The quotient digit goes above its place, the multiple is written under the working number and taken away, and a left slot takes what remains before the next digit can be brought down: the bring down arrow stays unlit until that slot is filled. A zero gate watches the quotient row. It takes a zero only when the working number is smaller than the divisor, and a zero offered at a step that is bigger than the divisor but leaves something over is handed back with the multiple strip lit to show that at least one fits. A check bar under the frame multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder and stands the result beside the dividend. A blocks bay along the foot holds three divisions to a block and adds their quotients, and its label says that the block's total is their sum.
source_tool.art_direction: A long division frame under place headings / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line

zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a tray of counters and a row of plates, digit cards under place headings, sticks tied in bundles, a long division frame with its bracket, a ladder of multiples, a strip of cells, a story card, and two rails tied at every stop.

Equal shares are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a plate or a part is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are on it, and anything counted one at a time is drawn in rows of ten so that no more than twenty loose things ever have to be counted singly.

What is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the shares, in a dish or a slot of its own, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never tucked under a share and never left to be guessed from a gap.
A division is always written with every place headed. The number being divided at a step is shown with its place name, so fifteen tens is never drawn as a bare fifteen.

Every zero in a quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as the other digits and is never dimmed, shrunk or dropped. A zero is written only where the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a leading zero may stand or be left off, but a zero after the first digit always stands.
What is left at every step is drawn in its own slot before the next digit comes down, and it slides down to join that digit so the next number can be seen being made.
A remainder is written as a number. A zero standing in front of its other digits is lifted off and set aside, never written into the answer.
No stage ever shows a number for a division by zero. Where one is asked, the stage says it is not possible and draws nothing to share into.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a counter, a digit or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; and what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion. Those four hold from the plates to the frame to the story card in every tool of this chapter. A multiple of the divisor, whether it is being tried on the ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose, so the chunks can be added up without being mistaken for the share. A zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey, and grey never means faint: it is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, because it is holding a place. All of that holds in greyscale, because what is left over is told apart by the dish or the left slot it sits in, and a quotient digit by the row it sits in, before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the working window with its place name, then lay the multiples beside it.
voice.onNext: A new division. Name the biggest place before anything is shared.
voice.opening: A number under its place headings, and a divisor at the door. Which place goes first?
voice.onFinish: Every step said, every zero where the number was smaller, and every check matched.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any dividend, any divisor from two to nine, with the gate and the check bar open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Smaller than the divisor means a zero

placement.where: After play money in hundreds, tens and ones has been shared into envelopes by hand, changing each left-over note for ten of the next. The tool is what will not bring a digit down until what is left has been said, and what refuses a zero at a step where the divisor fits, which a pencil on paper cannot refuse.

answer_key.rule: Start with the digit in the biggest place. Divide what is there by the divisor, write the quotient digit above that place, take the multiple away and say what is left. What is left joins the next digit brought down, and that is the next number to divide. When the number being divided at a step is smaller than the divisor, no divisor fits, so a zero goes in the quotient and the whole number is carried on. That is the only test. A step that leaves something over but is not smaller than the divisor still gets a digit of one or more. A zero before the first digit may be written or left off; a zero anywhere after it must be written. To check, multiply the divisor by the quotient and add the remainder; the answer is the dividend.
answer_key.wrong: The step is run again from its working window with the place name read aloud, the multiple strip is laid beside it, and the zero gate asks whether the working number is smaller than the divisor. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The biggest place is the hundreds: 8 hundreds divided by 3 is 2 hundreds, with 2 hundreds left.
The 2 hundreds left join the 4 tens to make 24 tens, and 24 tens divided by 3 is 8 tens.
6 ones divided by 3 is 2 ones, so 846 divided by 3 is 282 with nothing left over.
items.answer: Start with the 8 hundreds: 2 hundreds each, with 2 hundreds carried into the tens. The quotient is 282, remainder 0
items.question: Divide 846 by 3. Where do you start, and what is carried?
items.checkpoint: Long division starts with the digit in the biggest place, and whatever is left is carried into the next place.
items.misconception: Starting with the ones, as in adding and taking away, and building the quotient backwards.

steps: 9 hundreds divided by 4 is 2 hundreds, with 1 hundred left.
Bring down the 5 tens: 1 hundred and 5 tens make 15 tens, and 15 tens divided by 4 is 3 tens, with 3 tens left.
Bring down the 3 ones: 33 ones divided by 4 is 8 ones, with 1 left, so the answer is 238 remainder 1.
items.question: Divide 953 by 4, saying what is left at each step.
items.checkpoint: Each step brings down the next digit and divides everything that has built up.
items.misconception: Dividing the 5 tens on their own and forgetting the hundred that was left.

steps: 9 thousands divided by 7 is 1 thousand with 2 left. 9 is not smaller than 7, so the digit is 1 and not 0.
2 thousands and 8 hundreds make 28 hundreds, which is 4 hundreds with nothing left. Then 3 tens come down, and 3 is smaller than 7, so 0 tens, with 3 tens left.
3 tens and 6 ones make 36 ones, which is 5 ones with 1 left, so the answer is 1405 remainder 1.
items.answer: At the tens: 3 tens is smaller than 7, so a zero goes in the tens place. The answer is 1405 remainder 1
items.question: 9836 is divided by 7. At which step does a zero go in the quotient, and why? What is the answer?
items.checkpoint: A zero goes in the quotient only when the number being divided at that step is smaller than the divisor.
items.misconception: Writing a zero in the quotient at every step that leaves a remainder, because that step does not divide exactly.

steps: 5 thousands is smaller than 8, so the division starts with 51 hundreds: 6 hundreds, with 3 left.
37 tens divided by 8 is 4 tens, with 5 left, and 58 ones divided by 8 is 7, with 2 left.
Check: 8 times 647 is 5176, and adding the remainder 2 gives 5178, the dividend, so the answer is right.
items.answer: 647 remainder 2, and 8 times 647 is 5176, add 2 makes 5178
items.question: Divide 5178 by 8, and check the answer by multiplying back.
items.checkpoint: Divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives back the dividend; if it does not, a step went wrong.
items.misconception: Checking by multiplying the divisor by the quotient and forgetting to add the remainder.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Divide 915 by 5, saying what is left after each step.
items.final_answer: 183, with 4 hundreds left after the first step, 1 ten after the second and nothing at the end

items.question: In 612 divided by 6, what goes in the tens place of the quotient, and why?
items.final_answer: A zero, because 1 ten is smaller than 6; the quotient is 102

items.question: Divide 2736 by 4.
items.final_answer: 684, remainder 0. The 2 thousands are smaller than 4, so the division starts with 27 hundreds

items.question: Divide 8045 by 8.
items.final_answer: The quotient is 1005, remainder 5: a zero goes in the hundreds and a zero in the tens, because 0 hundreds and then 4 tens are each smaller than 8

items.question: Check by multiplying back whether 3097 divided by 6 is 516 remainder 1.
items.final_answer: Yes: 6 times 516 is 3096, and adding 1 gives 3097

items.question: A child says 7562 divided by 9 is 84 remainder 2. Multiply back to test it, then find the right answer.
items.final_answer: 9 times 84 is 756, add 2 makes 758, not 7562, so it is wrong. The quotient is 840 remainder 2: the last 2 ones are smaller than 9, so a zero goes in the ones place

items.question: One block of a stand has three rows. Row A seats 738 divided by 6 people, row B seats 856 divided by 8, and row C seats 935 divided by 5. The block holds the three rows added together. How many people is that?
items.final_answer: 417, because the rows seat 123, 107 and 187, and those add up to 417

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: shows the number being divided at each step, with its place name
lists the divisor times one up to times nine beside the window
takes each quotient digit above its own place
takes what is left after each step, and must be filled before the next digit comes down
brings the next digit down beside what is left, unlit until the left slot is filled
takes a zero only when the working number is smaller than the divisor
multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder and stands it beside the dividend
holds three divisions to a block and adds their quotients

teaching_notes: Share play money into envelopes before the tool is opened, hundreds first, changing any hundred that will not go round into ten tens, then the tens, then the ones. Ask when an envelope got none of a note, and why a zero goes in that place. Then use the tool for its two refusals. It will not bring a digit down until what is left has been said, because the leftover is where the next number comes from. And it will not take a zero at a step where the divisor fits. The summary box after the worked examples says a zero appears when a digit is not divisible by the divisor. Do not teach that sentence. The worked examples divide thirty-five hundreds and fifty-six tens by six, neither of them divisible, and write five and nine. The first example states the real test itself: three is smaller than five, so put a zero in the quotient. A child who follows the box writes a zero at every step that leaves a remainder, and ends with an answer full of zeros. Say the test the same way every time: smaller than the divisor, a zero; not smaller, at least one fits. The check at the end is the other half of the box, and it is right: divisor times quotient, add the remainder, gives the dividend. The blocks bay is practice in adding the answers of several one-digit divisions, and its label says that a block's total is the sum of its quotients; the seating circle on the closing skills page, which needs that same reading, is served by the two-digit tool, because most of its divisions are by ten or by a number with two digits.
generation_prompt: Build a long division tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A long division frame fills the working area, with the dividend written under place headings from thousands to ones and the divisor at its left behind a drawn bracket. A working window above the frame shows the number being divided at the current step together with its place name. A multiple strip beside the window lists the divisor times one to times nine, and the largest multiple that fits is chosen from it. Each quotient digit is written above its own place, the multiple is written under the working number and taken away, and a left slot takes what remains; the bring down arrow stays unlit until that slot is filled, and then brings the next digit down beside it. A zero gate watches the quotient row: it accepts a zero only when the working number is smaller than the divisor, and a zero offered at a step where the divisor fits is handed back with the fitting multiples lit on the strip, with nothing marked. A check bar under the frame multiplies the divisor by the quotient, adds the remainder, and slides the result under the dividend so the two can be matched digit for digit. A blocks bay along the foot of the canvas holds three divisions to a block and writes the sum of their quotients as the block's total, saying so in its label. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Start with the biggest place. Divide, write the digit on top, and say what is left. Bring the next digit down. If the number is smaller than the divisor, write a zero. Multiply back to check.
